periods.activity_title: Sky Watching: Drawing What We See
periods.textbook_anchor: Pictures of the Sky — Draw a picture of the sky as it appears in the morning, afternoon and at night (p. 152)

time_bands.activity: The teacher invites students to close their eyes and recall what the sky looks like at different times — early morning when they wake, bright afternoon, and after dark. Students share one word each that describes the sky at those times. The teacher collects words on the board without evaluating them, building curiosity about why the sky changes.

Students open Textbook p. 152 and draw three sky pictures — morning, afternoon, night — in the spaces provided, adding colour to show the sky's appearance at each time. They are encouraged to include the Sun, Moon, stars, or cloud shapes they genuinely recall or observe, rather than copying a neighbour.

Students hold up their drawings and the teacher guides a gallery walk around the room. Students notice similarities and differences — which colours appear at morning and afternoon, which objects appear only at night. The teacher points out that the Sun is so bright that all other stars become invisible while it is present, linking students' own drawings to this idea.

Each student writes one sentence below their night-sky drawing: something they notice about the sky that they would like to understand better. The teacher collects or asks two or three students to share aloud, affirming that wondering about the sky is where sky-study begins.

periods.implied_lo: Students can represent observed features of the natural environment through drawing and use those representations to notice patterns and differences.
periods.section_context: Sky colour changes across morning, afternoon, and night; Sun's brightness making other stars invisible; Moon's visible shape at night; student-drawn sky pictures.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Does everyone's morning sky look the same colour — why might some look orange and some pale blue?' This naturally surfaces that observation depends on exact time and local conditions, including clouds. Keep the drawing phase unhurried — children who linger on detail are doing the cognitive work.

periods.activity_title: Sky Observation Table: Recording Changes Across the Day
periods.textbook_anchor: Pictures of the Sky — Write down what you observe in the sky during the morning, afternoon and at night, in the table given below (p. 153)

time_bands.activity: The teacher poses the question: 'If you watched the sky all day long, what would change and what would stay the same?' Students talk in pairs for a brief moment, then the teacher collects two or three ideas on the board. This frames the recording task as checking a prediction, not just copying.

Students open Textbook p. 153 and work on the observation table, filling in what they observe in the sky during morning, afternoon, and night. The teacher draws attention to the pre-filled examples and asks students to add at least two new points of their own in the blank rows, drawing on their own daily experiences at home.

The teacher leads a whole-class discussion of the completed tables, writing student contributions under three columns on the board: Morning / Afternoon / Night. Students are guided to notice that the Sun's apparent colour (pale/orange/golden/white) and position shift across the day, and that animals and plants change their behaviour accordingly — birds that sing at dawn, flowers that open in sunlight, animals that come out at night.

Students discuss, as a class, observed changes during sunrise and sunset — how the sky looks, what birds and animals do, and what changes at home — drawing from the questions in Textbook p. 154. They add any new observations to their table that the discussion prompted.

periods.implied_lo: Students can record systematic observations of a natural phenomenon in a structured table and identify changes across different conditions.
periods.section_context: Sky colour and Sun position across morning, afternoon, and night; animal and plant behaviour changes; sunrise and sunset observations; textbook observation table.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'What does a rooster, a cow, or a flower do when the Sun rises — and what does that tell us about how living things respond to the sky?' This draws on students' home environments and invites diverse rural, urban, and regional observations without requiring any one answer.

periods.activity_title: Shadow Inquiry: Torch, Stick, and a Dark Room
periods.textbook_anchor: The Shadows — Take a torch and a stick; observe changes in the shadow as the stick moves and the torch direction changes (p. 156)
materials: A stick or pencil (one per group)
Dark cloth or ability to darken a corner of the room

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'What makes a shadow? Have you ever tried to make your shadow bigger or smaller?' Students share brief ideas. The teacher then introduces the inquiry: today the class will test what actually changes a shadow's size and direction, using a torch and a stick as their tools, following the activity in Textbook p. 156.

Students work in small groups. Each group darkens their corner or uses a desk torch, holds the stick upright, shines the torch on it, and carries out two tests: (a) moving the stick closer to and farther from the torch while observing the shadow, and (b) changing the direction the torch points while the stick stays still. Students record what they notice in their notebooks — a quick sketch of each setup and one sentence about what changed.

Groups report their findings. The teacher guides a whole-class synthesis: objects closer to the light source cast larger shadows; changing the light's direction changes the shadow's direction. The teacher then connects this to the Sun — the Sun is very far away but is the giant torch of the day, and as it moves from East to West, shadows shift in direction and in length.
Students write one sentence in their notebooks: 'Shadow size changes when… and shadow direction changes when…' This closes the inquiry on its own ground.

periods.implied_lo: Students can perform a simple inquiry to test how changing the position and direction of a light source affects the size and direction of a shadow.
periods.section_context: Shadow formation with torch and stick; shadow size change with distance from light source; shadow direction change with torch direction; connection to Sun's East-to-West movement.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If the Sun is very far away, why do we still get shadows? What does that tell us about how powerful sunlight is?' Prompt groups who finish quickly to predict what the shadow would look like if the torch were directly above the stick — this parallels the noon-Sun situation. Keep the inquiry phase unhurried so every group completes both tests before reporting.

periods.activity_title: Shadows Through the Day: Drawing Sun and Shadow Positions
periods.textbook_anchor: The Shadows — Draw the position of the Sun and corresponding shadows in the images given below (p. 157)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks students to stand near the window briefly and observe where the light is coming from. She then asks: 'If I stood outside right now, where would my shadow fall?' This grounds the drawing task in immediate experience. The class reviews the key ideas from the torch inquiry — closer light makes bigger shadow, light direction determines shadow direction — as a foundation for the drawing task.

Students open Textbook p. 157 and draw the position of the Sun and the corresponding shadows in each image provided — for morning, noon, and evening scenes. They annotate each drawing with a word or phrase: 'long shadow', 'short shadow', 'shadow falls East', 'shadow falls West', to make their reasoning visible.

The teacher invites two or three students to share their drawings on the board or hold them up. The class checks: Does the shadow point away from the Sun? Is the noon shadow the shortest? The teacher introduces the Jantar Mantar connection here — ancient people in India noticed exactly this pattern, and Raja Jai Singh built observatories in five cities so that the Samrat Yantra's shadow could tell the time accurately. Shadow puppetry, too, is an art form that has used the behaviour of shadows for generations.

Students write one question about shadows or sundials that they would like to ask — anything that occurred to them during the drawing or discussion. The teacher collects these to affirm curiosity as a scientific value.

periods.implied_lo: Students can represent the relationship between a light source's position and the direction and length of a shadow through labelled diagrams.
periods.section_context: Sun position at morning, noon, and evening; corresponding shadow direction and length; Jantar Mantar observatories and Samrat Yantra sundial; shadow puppetry as traditional art form.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Why do you think Raja Jai Singh needed to build such a large structure just to read time from a shadow — what does that tell you about how carefully people watched the sky?' This opens the cultural strand naturally and invites students to appreciate that sky observation has practical and artistic value across human history.

periods.activity_title: The Night Sky: Observing and Drawing Star Patterns and Moon Shapes
periods.textbook_anchor: Night Sky — Observe the Moon in the sky and draw the shapes of the Moon you have observed on different nights (p. 160)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'Has anyone ever looked at the night sky and seen a pattern in the stars — like a shape or a picture?' Students share briefly. The teacher introduces the idea that people across many cultures have seen pictures in star groupings for thousands of years, and that Indian tradition names one group the Saptarshi — the Seven Sages. Students are asked to draw the star pattern they most remember seeing or would draw if they imagined the night sky.

Students open Textbook p. 160 and draw the shapes of the Moon they have observed on different nights, filling in the provided spaces. For each Moon shape they draw, they write its name if they know it — full circle, crescent, half — or invent a descriptive word. The teacher circulates, asking students to recall which shape they saw most recently and whether they remember which shape comes before or after.

The class discusses the textbook's questions: Is there a pattern to the Moon's changing shape? Are there nights when the Moon is not visible? The teacher introduces the names Poornima (full Moon), Amavasya (new Moon/no Moon), and the crescent shape, and explains that ancient peoples used these changes to count days — this is how the earliest calendars were born. The teacher notes that many festivals across India and the world are tied to these Moon shapes.

Students write two observations in their notebooks: one about a star pattern they know or imagine, and one about the Moon's shape on a night they remember. This is a personal record, not a right-or-wrong task.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe and record changes in the appearance of a celestial object over time and describe the pattern those changes follow.
periods.section_context: Star patterns in the night sky; Saptarshi (Seven Sages) star pattern; Moon phases — Poornima (full Moon), crescent, half-Moon, Amavasya (no Moon); Moon shape used to count days and create earliest calendars.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Does your family ever notice the Moon's shape on special evenings — perhaps before a festival or when elders mention something?' This draws out students' lived knowledge of lunar timekeeping without framing it as a separate topic. Students from different regions may name different star patterns or Moon-related customs — welcome all of these.

periods.activity_title: Moon, Festivals, and Calendars: Connecting Sky Patterns to Cultural Life
periods.textbook_anchor: Night Sky — Do you celebrate any festivals in your family or community related to the Sun or the Moon? What do you call them in your language? (p. 162)

time_bands.activity: The teacher writes on the board: 'Poornima — Amavasya — First Crescent' and asks students which of these Moon shapes they associate with any celebration or special day in their home or community. Students call out names freely — the teacher lists them without evaluating, building a rich diverse display on the board.

Students open Textbook p. 162 and write their response to the question about festivals in their family or community related to the Sun or Moon, including what they call these festivals in their own language. The teacher then facilitates a structured class sharing: for each Moon phase on the board, which festivals were named? The chapter's examples — Diwali on Amavasya, Rakshabandhan/Guru Poornima/Buddha Poornima on Poornima, Eid on the first crescent — are introduced as additional examples, not as the only correct answers.

The teacher poses the connecting question: 'Why do you think people chose the Moon — rather than something else — to organise festivals and count time?' Students discuss in pairs, then share. The teacher weaves in the idea that the Moon's shape change is visible, reliable, and happens over a period that is long enough to plan but short enough to track — making it the first natural calendar that humans used, long before any written record.

Students write one sentence summarising the connection they find most interesting between a Moon phase and a festival or tradition. These sentences are shared aloud by two or three volunteers to close the unit.

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe the relationship between an observed natural pattern and a cultural practice or tradition in their community.
periods.section_context: Moon phases — Poornima, Amavasya, first crescent; festivals linked to Moon phases — Diwali, Rakshabandhan, Guru Poornima, Buddha Poornima, Eid; Moon-phase calendars as earliest timekeeping; students' own community festivals tied to Sun or Moon.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Why might two different communities celebrate a festival on the same Moon phase but call it a completely different name — what does that tell us about how people use the same sky in their own ways?' Expect and celebrate regional variation; students from different states or religious backgrounds may name many festivals not listed in the textbook — all are valid and enrich the discussion.

periods.activity_title: Chandrayaan and Sky Questions: India's Moon Mission and Scientific Curiosity
periods.textbook_anchor: India's Chandrayaan Mission — List at least two questions that Meera can ask her teacher about the Sun's apparent East-to-West movement (p. 162)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'Has anyone heard of Chandrayaan? What do you think it did?' Students share what they know. The teacher briefly introduces the Vikram Lander's landing on the Moon on 23 August 2023 and explains that India's scientists sent a spacecraft to the Moon to learn about its surface — the same Moon students have been observing and drawing. This connects personal sky observation to national scientific achievement.

Students turn to Textbook p. 162 and work on the Meera task: listing at least two questions Meera can ask her teacher about why the Sun appears to move from East to West during the day. Students write their questions individually in notebooks first, then share with a partner to compare. The teacher collects examples on the board — good scientific questions include 'why', 'how', 'what if', and 'does it always' starters.

The teacher also draws out the comparison task from Textbook p. 162 — two differences between day and night, morning sky and evening sky, our activities during day and night, and animal activities during day and night. Students discuss these comparisons in pairs and share one or two for each category. This consolidates the natural strand across the whole chapter.

Students write one question of their own — about the Moon, the Sun, Chandrayaan, or anything from the sky that they genuinely wonder about. The teacher reads two or three aloud and affirms that asking such questions is exactly what scientists do.

periods.implied_lo: Students can formulate questions about observed patterns in the natural world and use comparisons to distinguish related phenomena.
periods.section_context: Chandrayaan mission; Vikram Lander Moon landing on 23 August 2023; Sun's apparent East-to-West movement; day-and-night differences; morning-sky and evening-sky comparison; day and night activity differences for humans and animals.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If you could send one question to the scientists who built Chandrayaan, what would you ask them about the Moon?' This elevates students' curiosity to a scientific level and connects the cultural pride of India's space programme to their own wonder. Students who have read the Grade 3 English or Hindi textbooks may already know about Chandrayaan — invite them to share what they recall.

periods.activity_title: Sky Poem and Shadow Riddle: Expressing Sky Learning Through Creative Writing
periods.textbook_anchor: India's Chandrayaan Mission — Write your own poem inspired by the beauty of the sky (p. 163)

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads aloud the riddle from Textbook p. 163: 'Only one colour, but not one size / Appears with light, looks very nice.' She asks students to guess the answer and complete the next two lines of the riddle themselves. Students call out ideas — the class discusses why the answer fits all the clues — bridging shadow and sky knowledge into a playful format.

Students complete the riddle individually in their notebooks, writing the missing lines and the answer. The teacher invites two or three volunteers to read their completed riddles aloud. The class appreciates that different students completed the riddle differently and that more than one version can be equally good.

Students turn to Textbook p. 163 and write their own poem inspired by the beauty of the sky. The teacher suggests they can draw on any image from what they have observed and discussed — the changing colours at sunrise, a crescent Moon over rooftops, stars forming a pattern, a shadow shrinking at noon — and that the poem can be as short as four lines or as long as they wish. Students who prefer may draw an illustrated poem where the picture carries some of the meaning.

A poetry sharing circle: students sit together and volunteers read their poems aloud. The teacher notes images that are particularly vivid or surprising, and affirms that using the sky as a subject for art and poetry is something people have done across every culture and every time period.

Students write their name on their poem page and the teacher collects notebooks, or students keep them to share at home. The unit closes with the observation that the sky has inspired both science and art — and that being curious about it puts students in the company of every astronomer, poet, and sky-watcher who came before them.

periods.implied_lo: Students can express observations and ideas about the natural world through a creative written form, selecting images and language that communicate what they have noticed.
periods.section_context: Sky-inspired poem; shadow riddle completion; sunrise colours; crescent Moon; star patterns; shadow shrinking at noon; creative expression about sky observations.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'What is one thing about the sky that you noticed this term that you had never thought about before?' This invites genuine reflection. Students who are reluctant writers can draw an illustrated poem — accept any form that shows they are reaching for words or images to express sky ideas. Avoid correcting poetic choices; affirm specificity and genuine observation over conventional rhyme.

assessment_items.task: Look at the sky right now — or recall clearly what it looked like this morning. Draw the sky in that moment and write three things you notice about it: the colours you see, whether you can spot the Sun or Moon, and one thing that might have looked different at another time of day.
assessment_items.scaffold: My sky drawing: [draw here]. Three things I notice: 1. The colour is ___. 2. I can / cannot see the Sun or Moon because ___. 3. At a different time of day it might look ___ because ___.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any accurate sky colour or feature. Look for the student connecting time-of-day to sky appearance. A strong response names a specific colour change and gives a reason; a weak response draws without written observation or copies without personal detail.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can represent observed features of the natural environment through drawing and use those representations to notice patterns and differences.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can use drawing as an observational tool and connect a sky feature to a time-of-day pattern, showing that representation and pattern-noticing work together.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Check that the student filled all three sentence stems with genuine observation, not generic phrases. The third stem ('at a different time…') is the key pattern-noticing prompt.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: specific colour named (orange, pale blue, deep black), a reason given for Sun or Moon visibility, and a plausible time-of-day contrast. Weak: drawing only with no writing, or writing 'the sky is blue' without connecting to time of day.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who have difficulty writing may dictate their three observations to the teacher or a peer who scribes. Students who are colourblind may describe brightness and object-visibility rather than colour.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Drawing plus writing mirrors the textbook task and honours the chapter's dual visual-verbal approach to sky observation.

assessment_items.question_text: Ravi is filling in his sky observation table. He notices that in the morning column he wrote 'many stars visible', but in the afternoon column he cannot think of any stars to list. Which explanation best fits what Ravi has observed?

options.label: A
options.text: Clouds always cover the stars in the afternoon.

options.label: B
options.text: Stars move to the other side of the Earth during the day.

options.label: C
options.text: Stars only exist at night and disappear in the morning.

options.label: D
options.text: The Sun is so bright during the day that other stars cannot be seen even though they are still there.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer: B. This tests whether students have internalised the chapter's core explanation for star invisibility during the day — the Sun's overwhelming brightness — rather than holding a misconception that stars physically vanish.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can record systematic observations of a natural phenomenon in a structured table and identify changes across different conditions.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing A reveals a spatial misconception — the student thinks stars physically move to a hidden location during daytime rather than understanding that their light is outshone.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing C reveals a more fundamental misconception — the student believes stars cease to exist during the day, not grasping that stars are always present but rendered invisible by sunlight.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing D reveals that the student is confusing cloud cover (a weather event) with the systematic daily disappearance of stars, showing incomplete engagement with the observation table's day/night pattern.

assessment_items.question_text: Priya sets up a torch and a stick in a darkened corner. She moves the stick closer to the torch. What change does she observe in the shadow? Then she keeps the stick still and turns the torch to point in a different direction. What change does she observe now? Write one observation for each situation.
expected_elements: When the stick is moved closer to the torch, the shadow becomes larger (or: the shadow grows bigger / the shadow increases in size).
When the torch is pointed in a different direction, the shadow also moves to a different direction (or: the shadow direction changes / the shadow falls on a different side).
assessment_items.annotation: Award one mark for each correctly identified change. Accept any phrasing that correctly states size increase for closer distance and direction change for torch direction change. Do not penalise informal language.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can perform a simple inquiry to test how changing the position and direction of a light source affects the size and direction of a shadow.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: Shadow becomes larger when the stick is moved closer to the torch.
Shadow direction changes when the torch is pointed in a different direction.

assessment_items.question_text: Look at the three situations below. For each one, write whether the shadow will be long or short, and in which direction it will fall (towards the East or towards the West). Situation 1: Early morning, Sun is low in the East. Situation 2: Noon, Sun is directly overhead. Situation 3: Late evening, Sun is low in the West.
expected_elements: Situation 1 (early morning): Shadow is long and falls towards the West (away from the Sun in the East).
Situation 2 (noon): Shadow is shortest (Sun is overhead / directly above).
Situation 3 (late evening): Shadow is long and falls towards the East (away from the Sun in the West).
assessment_items.annotation: Award one mark per situation for a fully correct response (both length and direction correct). Accept 'very small' for noon shadow. A student who gets direction correct but length wrong, or vice versa, may receive half credit at teacher discretion.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can represent the relationship between a light source's position and the direction and length of a shadow through labelled diagrams.

competency.competency_text: Asks questions and makes predictions about simple patterns (season change, food chain, phases of the moon, movement of stars and planets, shapes of trees, plants, leaves, and flowers, rituals, celebrations) observed in the immediate environment

expected_elements: Morning shadow: long, falls towards the West.
Noon shadow: shortest / very short (direction may be any, as Sun is overhead).
Evening shadow: long, falls towards the East.

assessment_items.question_text: Ananya observes the Moon on four different nights and draws what she sees each time. Which of the following best describes the correct order of Moon shapes across a lunar month?

options.label: A
options.text: The Moon changes shape randomly with no pattern.

options.label: B
options.text: The Moon is always full but appears as a crescent when clouds partly cover it.

options.label: C
options.text: The Moon stays the same shape every night and only sometimes hides behind clouds.

options.label: D
options.text: The Moon's shape changes gradually from no Moon (Amavasya) to a crescent, then to a half-Moon, then to a full Moon (Poornima), and then back again.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer: B. Tests whether students have internalised that Moon phases follow a predictable cyclical pattern, not random or weather-dependent variation.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe and record changes in the appearance of a celestial object over time and describe the pattern those changes follow.

competency.competency_text: Asks questions and makes predictions about simple patterns (season change, food chain, phases of the moon, movement of stars and planets, shapes of trees, plants, leaves, and flowers, rituals, celebrations) observed in the immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing A reveals the student has not engaged with the Moon-shape observation task and holds the misconception that clouds explain Moon visibility rather than Moon phases.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing C shows the student observed that the Moon changes shape but missed the pattern entirely — they need more structured observation across consecutive nights.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing D reveals a cloud-cover misconception specifically about the crescent: the student thinks the crescent is a full Moon partially hidden, not a genuine phase of the Moon's illumination cycle.

assessment_items.question_text: Many festivals in India are celebrated on a full Moon night (Poornima) or on a no-Moon night (Amavasya). Why do you think people chose the Moon's shape to decide when to celebrate festivals? Give at least two reasons and name one festival for each Moon phase you mention.
look_for: Student explains that the Moon's shape change is visible to everyone without special instruments, making it a reliable natural marker.
Student notes that the cycle is predictable — the Moon returns to the same shape regularly — allowing people to plan in advance.
Student names at least one festival correctly matched to a Moon phase (e.g., Diwali on Amavasya, Rakshabandhan or Guru Poornima on Poornima, Eid on first crescent after Amavasya).
Student shows awareness that different communities use the same Moon phases for different festivals, reflecting diversity of cultural practice.
assessment_items.annotation: This is an open-reasoning item. Award marks for quality of reasoning, not for listing the most festivals. Regional variation is expected and valid — a student who names a regional festival not listed in the textbook but correctly matched to a Moon phase should receive full credit for that point. Do not penalise for spelling of festival names.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe the relationship between an observed natural pattern and a cultural practice or tradition in their community.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

look_for: Identification of Moon's visibility as a shared, instrument-free natural marker accessible to all people.
Recognition that the Moon's phase cycle is predictable and therefore useful for planning celebrations.
Correct pairing of at least one festival with its Moon phase (Diwali–Amavasya, or Rakshabandhan/Guru Poornima/Buddha Poornima–Poornima, or Eid–first crescent).
Any acknowledgement that different traditions use the same Moon phases, showing cultural diversity within a shared natural phenomenon.

assessment_items.question_text: Meera is curious about a statement her teacher made: 'The Sun appears to move from East to West during the day.' Write two questions that Meera could ask her teacher to find out more about this.
expected_elements: A question that probes why or how the Sun appears to move (e.g., 'Why does the Sun appear to move from East to West?' or 'Is the Sun actually moving or is something else causing this?').

A question that probes evidence or observation related to the Sun's apparent movement (e.g., 'How can we tell the direction the Sun is moving from?' or 'Does the Sun always rise in exactly the same place in the East every day?').
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any genuine scientific question about the Sun's apparent East-to-West movement. Do not require technical vocabulary. The key criterion is that the question probes the phenomenon rather than simply restating it. Award one mark per valid question.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can formulate questions about observed patterns in the natural world and use comparisons to distinguish related phenomena.

competency.competency_text: Asks questions and makes predictions about simple patterns (season change, food chain, phases of the moon, movement of stars and planets, shapes of trees, plants, leaves, and flowers, rituals, celebrations) observed in the immediate environment

expected_elements: A causal or mechanistic question about the Sun's apparent motion (why/how it appears to move).
An observational or evidence-seeking question about the Sun's position or direction at specific times of day.

assessment_items.task: Write a short poem (at least four lines) about something you have observed in the sky — the Sun, the Moon, stars, shadows, or colours at sunrise or sunset. Your poem should include at least one specific thing you actually noticed, not just a general description.
assessment_items.scaffold: My poem title: ___. My poem: [write here]. The specific thing I noticed that I put in my poem: ___.
format_of_output: A poem of at least four lines about a sky observation
One sentence identifying the specific observation included in the poem
assessment_items.annotation: Do not assess rhyme or poetic convention. Assess whether the poem contains at least one identifiable, specific observation from the sky (a colour, a shape, a movement, a behaviour of an animal at a sky-related time). A strong poem is specific; a weak poem stays purely generic ('the sky is beautiful, the stars are bright'). Accept any language the student chooses.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can express observations and ideas about the natural world through a creative written form, selecting images and language that communicate what they have noticed.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can translate a genuine observational memory into a creative written form, showing that sky learning is personal and expressible, not only factual.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The identification sentence at the end is the diagnostic key — if the student can name what specific observation they put in, they demonstrate that the poem is grounded in real noticing rather than generic phrasing.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: poem includes a specific sensory detail (colour named, shape described, animal behaviour mentioned) and the identification sentence matches something in the poem. Weak: poem uses only very general phrases with no specific observation, or identification sentence is left blank.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find writing challenging may dictate their poem to a peer or the teacher who scribes. Students may also draw an illustrated poem where images carry meaning alongside minimal words. Students may write in any language and translate a key phrase.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Poetry is the explicit creative mode named in the textbook task; the identification sentence makes the observational grounding of the poem visible to the teacher without requiring literary analysis.
